code.title: Value categories: what each expression is

followUps:
A string literal is an lvalue. It is an array object that lives for the whole program, so you can take its address: &"hi" is legal. By contrast 42 or 'a' are prvalues with no address.

That is why const char (&r)[3] = "hi"; compiles.

It is an xvalue. A member of a temporary object is itself expiring, so the language marks it as movable. By contrast, plain f() is a prvalue.

This is why std::string s = f().name; moves the string out of the temporary instead of copying it. Time: the move is O(1) for a string with heap storage, compared to O(n) for a copy.

Wrap the expression in double parentheses: decltype((e)) gives T& for an lvalue, T&& for an xvalue and plain T for a prvalue. With a bare name, decltype(x) gives the declared type instead.

int x = 0;
decltype((x))        // int&
decltype((x + 1))    // int
decltype((std::move(x))) // int&&

Pair it with static_assert(std::is_same_v<...>) to check it at build time.

code.title: What std::move really does

followUps:
Because it blocks copy elision and can force a move you did not need. When you write return local; the compiler may build the object directly in the caller (NRVO) at zero cost, and if it cannot, it still treats local as an rvalue and moves it.

return std::move(local); changes the expression type to T&&, so NRVO is disabled and you always pay one move. GCC and Clang warn with -Wpessimizing-move and -Wredundant-move.

It finds reads of an object after it was moved from, such as calling s.size() or using s in a loop after take(std::move(s)). The state of a moved-from object is valid but unspecified, so such a read usually gives a surprising value.

auto t = std::move(s);
use(s);        // flagged
s = "new";     // fine: reinitialised

It treats assignment, clear() and reset() as reinitialisation and stops warning after them.

code.title: Move constructor and assignment for a raw buffer

followUps:
Copy-and-swap takes the argument by value and swaps it with *this, so the copy constructor does the hard work and the old data is freed by the temporary's destructor.

Buf& operator=(Buf o) noexcept {
  std::swap(p_, o.p_);
  std::swap(n_, o.n_);
  return *this;
}

It is exception safe (if the copy throws, *this is untouched) and handles self-assignment correctly. One signature also covers copy and move assignment, at the price of one extra move for rvalues.

Declaring a destructor (even = default) suppresses the implicit move constructor and move assignment. The implicit copies are still generated, but deprecated, so moves silently turn into copies.

Declaring a copy operation also suppresses moves, and declaring a move operation deletes the implicit copies. Example: struct S { std::vector<int> v; ~S() {} }; copies a 1000 element vector when you write S b(std::move(a));. Fix by following Rule of 0, or by defaulting all five.

code.title: Rule of 5 versus Rule of 0 in practice

followUps:
Not automatically. ~T() = default; counts as user-declared, so the implicit move operations are not generated and std::move falls back to copying. The program stays correct but gets slower.

If you want the destructor and still want moves, write them out:

~T() = default;
T(T&&) = default;
T& operator=(T&&) = default;
T(const T&) = default;
T& operator=(const T&) = default;

Delete the copy operations and default the moves. Deleting the copy constructor and copy assignment is enough to suppress implicit copies, but it is clearer to write all four.

T(const T&) = delete;
T& operator=(const T&) = delete;
T(T&&) noexcept = default;
T& operator=(T&&) noexcept = default;

The easy way is to hold a member that is itself move-only, such as std::unique_ptr; a class with only such members and no declared special members is move-only automatically.

code.title: Vector growth: noexcept move or copy

followUps:
Node-based containers (list, map, set) never relocate elements, because each element lives in its own heap node that stays put. Growing only links a new node, so no copy or move happens and the move-noexcept issue does not arise.

std::deque also keeps existing elements in place: it stores fixed-size blocks and adds new blocks, so push_back does not move old elements (only the small block-pointer table grows). The cost is slower indexing and worse cache locality than vector.

It is a proposal to say a type can be moved by copying its raw bytes, then destroying the old location without running any code. That lets vector grow with a single memcpy instead of a move constructor plus destructor per element.

Types such as unique_ptr are trivially relocatable in practice, but the standard cannot assume it for every type (a type that stores its own address is not). Libraries such as folly and Abseil already use opt-in markers; it avoids per-element work for large vectors.

code.title: Perfect forwarding with make_unique

followUps:
Reference collapsing means that a reference to a reference collapses to one reference. Only && plus && stays an rvalue reference; all other mixes become an lvalue reference.

  1. T& & becomes T&
  2. T& && becomes T&
  3. T&& & becomes T&
  4. T&& && becomes T&&

This is why f(x) with an lvalue deduces T = int& and the parameter T&& becomes int&.

Forwarding fails whenever the argument cannot be deduced as a single type. Common cases:

  • Braced lists {1,2}: no type to deduce (use a named initializer_list).
  • 0 or NULL as null pointer: deduced as int, so use nullptr.
  • Overloaded function names or templates: the compiler cannot pick one overload.
  • Bit-fields: you cannot bind a non-const reference to them.

The direct call f({1,2}) works, but fwd({1,2}) does not.

A constructor like template<class T> Person(T&& n) is an exact match for non-const lvalues, while the copy constructor needs const Person&. So Person q(p); with a non-const p picks the template, which then tries to build a string from a Person and fails to compile.

Fix it by constraining the template, for example requires (!std::is_same_v<std::remove_cvref_t<T>, Person>) (or std::enable_if before C++20).

code.title: std::forward versus std::move

followUps:
After the first forward the object may already be moved from, so the second use sees an empty or unspecified value. Forwarding an rvalue means "you may steal it".

template<class T> void f(T&& x) {
  g(std::forward<T>(x));
  h(std::forward<T>(x)); // bug if x was an rvalue
}

If you call it with std::string("abc"), g may take the string, and h gets an empty one. Forward only at the last use, and pass an lvalue x to the earlier calls.

std::forward_like<T>(x) casts x to the value category and constness of T instead of its own. It is meant for forwarding a member of an object according to how the object itself was passed.

template<class Self> auto&& get(Self&& self) {
  return std::forward_like<Self>(self.value);
}

If self is an rvalue, you get an rvalue member; if self is const lvalue, you get a const lvalue. It is mainly used with deducing this.

code.title: Lambda captures and what they cost

followUps:
A by-value capture is stored in a closure member, and the closure's operator() is const by default, so it cannot change its members. mutable removes the const so you can change the lambda's own copy.

int x = 1;
auto f = [x]() mutable { return ++x; };
f(); f();   // returns 2 then 3; outer x is still 1

The state is kept between calls in that closure, but the original variable is never touched.

Only a lambda with no captures converts to a plain function pointer, because it then has no data members and its operator() can be exposed as a normal function. A capturing lambda needs somewhere to keep its state, which a bare function pointer cannot hold.

int (*fp)(int) = [](int a) { return a + 1; };  // ok
int k = 2;
// int (*bad)(int) = [k](int a) { return a + k; }; // error

Add unary plus, +[](int a){...}, to force the conversion in deduced contexts.

std::function is slower and bigger: it type-erases the callable behind a virtual-style call and may allocate on the heap if the closure is large. A variable of type auto holds the exact closure type, so the call can be inlined, with no allocation.

Use auto or a template parameter for local use and hot paths. Use std::function only when you must store different callables under one type (callbacks in a vector, class members). Expect roughly one indirect call (a few ns) plus possible allocation per construction.

code.title: Escaping lambdas: weak and strong self capture

followUps:
A keep-alive capture makes a cycle when the object stores the callback that holds a shared_ptr back to itself. Each keeps the other alive, so the reference count never reaches zero and the object leaks.

struct Conn : enable_shared_from_this<Conn> {
  std::function<void()> cb;
  void init() { cb = [self = shared_from_this()] {}; }
};

Break it with weak_from_this() for stored callbacks, or clear cb when done. A callback that is only queued and then discarded is not a cycle.

No, it is not safe unless the characters outlive the lambda. A string_view is just a pointer plus a length; copying it copies the pointer, not the text.

std::string s = "hello";
std::string_view v = s;
auto f = [v] { return v.size(); };
s.clear(); s.shrink_to_fit(); // v may now dangle

If the callback runs later, capture a std::string copy (or the owner via a shared_ptr) instead, so the data is owned by the closure.

code.title: auto, decltype and decltype(auto) deduction

followUps:
For vector<bool> the operator[] returns a proxy object (vector<bool>::reference), not a bool&, because bits are packed. So auto b = v[0]; deduces the proxy type.

The proxy still points into the vector, so it can dangle after a reallocation, and b = true may write through to the vector. Write bool b = v[0]; to get a real copy, or use static_cast<bool>(v[0]).

A trailing return type lets the return type use the parameter names, and it keeps the name of a class member in scope. It is needed when the type depends on the arguments.

template<class A, class B>
auto add(A a, B b) -> decltype(a + b) {
  return a + b;
}

Also used with lambdas that return a braced or ambiguous type, for example []() -> std::vector<int> { return {1}; }. Since C++14 plain auto return is often enough.

code.title: Structured bindings: copy versus alias

followUps:
A class with private members opts in by providing three pieces: a std::tuple_size specialisation, a std::tuple_element specialisation and a get<I> function (member or free function that finds it by ADL).

template<> struct std::tuple_size<Rgb>
  : std::integral_constant<size_t, 3> {};
// plus tuple_element and get<I>(const Rgb&)

The compiler then uses get instead of looking at the data members, so privacy does not matter. Without these, it only binds public data members of a plain aggregate.

Because auto [k, v] declares by value, the hidden variable e is a copy of each pair<const K, V>. For a map of strings that is one string copy per element.

Use for (const auto& [k, v] : m) to read, or auto& to modify values. Writing v = 100 in the by-value loop changes only the copy and leaves the map unchanged, as the program above shows (a stays 1).

code.title: const, constexpr, consteval, constinit

followUps:
Yes. Since C++20, a constexpr function may use new and delete, and std::vector and std::string are usable at compile time, but the memory must be freed before the evaluation ends.

constexpr int sum() {
  std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3};
  return v[0] + v[1] + v[2];
}
static_assert(sum() == 6);

The vector lives and dies inside the call. Returning the vector as a constexpr variable is not allowed, since the allocation would leak into runtime.

It lets one function have two bodies: one used when the call is evaluated at compile time, another for run time (for example a simple portable version for the compiler and a fast intrinsic at run time).

constexpr int f(int n) {
  if consteval { return slow(n); }
  else { return fast(n); }
}

std::is_constant_evaluated() is the older C++20 form. Inside if constexpr it is always true, which is a classic bug, so prefer if consteval (C++23).

code.title: optional, variant and any in use

followUps:
valueless_by_exception reports a variant that holds no value because a type-changing assignment or emplace threw an exception after the old value had been destroyed. It is rare, and only possible when an alternative's constructor or move can throw.

In that state index() equals std::variant_npos and std::visit throws bad_variant_access. Making all alternatives nothrow-move constructible avoids it entirely.

variant makes it easy to add a new operation (write another visit function) but hard to add a new type, since every visitor must be updated. Virtual inheritance is the opposite: a new type is a new subclass, but a new operation means touching every class.

Use variant for a closed, stable set of cases (AST nodes, protocol messages), and virtual functions when third parties add types. Variant also stores values inline with no heap allocation and no pointer chasing.

code.title: Lazy range views and dangling

followUps:
A sentinel is an end marker that need not be an iterator of the same type. It only has to be comparable with the iterator, which lets a range say "stop at the null character" without first scanning to find the end.

struct NulEnd {};
bool operator==(const char* p, NulEnd) { return *p == 0; }
// range: { const char* first; NulEnd last; }

It also makes infinite ranges such as views::iota(1) possible, since the end is a type that never compares equal.

It stops you from using an iterator into a temporary range that is already destroyed. When you pass an rvalue container to a range algorithm, it returns std::ranges::dangling instead of an iterator, so the code does not compile if you try to dereference it.

auto it = std::ranges::find(make_vec(), 3);
// *it;  // error: dangling has no operator*
auto v = make_vec();
auto ok = std::ranges::find(v, 3); // fine

Borrowed ranges (such as string_view and span) are exempt, since they do not own the data.

code.title: Guaranteed elision versus NRVO

followUps:
The compiler cannot apply NRVO when it does not know which object is returned at the time of construction. The named object must be the same on every return path.

  • Several different named locals returned on different branches.
  • Returning a parameter or a global, since those already exist in the caller's frame.
  • Returning a member or a conditional expression like c ? a : b.

In these cases the return is a move (or a copy if no move exists), as the noNrvo example above prints MOVE. Returning one object on all paths, or a prvalue, avoids the problem.

Temporary materialisation is the step where a prvalue is turned into an object (an xvalue) when it is actually needed, for example when you bind it to a reference, call a member function on it, or access a member.

struct S { int m; int get() const; };
S make();
int a = make().m;     // materialised here
const S& r = make();  // lifetime extended
int b = make().get(); // object exists for the call

Before that point a prvalue is only a recipe, which is why T x = T(); needs no copy or move.
